title: Men the Greeks made into gods
source_text: Οὐδὲν δὲ εἶδος τοῦ περὶ ἡμῶν διασυρμοῦ καὶ καταγέλωτος καταλιπὼν ὁ βωμολόχος Κέλσος ἐν τῷ καθ᾿ ἡμῶν λόγῳ Διοσκούρους καὶ Ἡρακλέα καὶ Ἀσκληπιὸν καὶ Διόνυσον ὀνομάζει, τοὺς ἐξ ἀνθρώπων πεπιστευμένους παρ᾿ Ἕλλησι γεγονέναι θεοὺς. καὶ φησιν οὐκ ἀνέχεσθαι μὲν ἡμᾶς τούτους νομίζειν θεοὺς. ὅτι ἄνθρωποι ἦσαν καὶ πρῶτοι. καίτοι πολλὰ ἐπιδειξαμένους καὶ γενναῖα ὑπὲρ ἀνθρώπων· τὸν δ᾿ Ἰησοῦν ἀποθανόντα ὑπὸ τῶν ἰδίων θιασωτῶν ὦφθαί φαμεν· προσκατηγορεῖ δ᾿ ἡμῶν καὶ ὡς λεγόντων αὐτὸν ὦφθαι, καὶ ταῦτα σκιάν. καὶ πρὸς ταῦτα δὲ φήσομεν ὅτι δεινῶς ὁ Κέλσος οὔτε σαφῶς παρέστησε μὴ σέβειν τούτους ὡς θεοὺς (εὐλαβεῖτο γὰρ τὴν δόξαν τῶν ἐντευξομένων αὐτοῦ τῇ γραφῇ. ὑποληψομένων αὐτὸν ἄθεον, εἴ τι τῆς φαινομένης αὐτῷ ἀληθείας ἐπρέσβευεν). οὔτ᾿ αὖ προσεποιήσατο καὶ αὐτὸς αὐτοὺς θεοὺς νομίζειν· πρὸς ἑκάτερον γὰρ ἂν αὐτῶν ἀπεκρινάμεθα. φέρε οὖν πρὸς μὲν τοὺς μὴ νομίζοντας αὐτοὺς εἶναι θεοὺς ταῦτ᾿ εἴπωμεν. ἆρ᾿ οὐδὲ τὴν ἀρχήν εἰσιν οὗτοι, ἀλλ᾿, ὥσπερ οἴονταί τινες περὶ τῆς τῶν ἀνθρώπων ψυχῆς ὡς παραχρῆμα διαφθειρομένης, διεφθάρη καὶ τούτων ἡ ψυχή· ἢ κατὰ τὴν δόξαν τῶν λεγόντων ἐπιδιαμένειν ἢ ἀθάνατον αὐτὴν εἶναι ἐπιδιαμένουσιν οὗτοι ἢ ἀθάνατοί εἰσι, καὶ θεοὶ μὲν οὐκ εἰσὶν ἥρωες δέ· ἢ οὐδὲ ἥρωες ἀλλ᾿ ἁπαξαπλῶς ψυχαί; εἰ μὲν οὖν οὐκ εἶναι ὑπολαμβάνετε αὐτοὺς. τὸν προηγούμενον ἡμῖν περὶ ψυχῆς κατασκευαστέον λόγον· εἰ δὲ εἰσὶ, καὶ οὕτω τὸν περὶ ἀθανασίας ἀποδεκτέον οὐ μόνον ἐκ τῶν καλῶς περὶ αὐτῆς εἰπόντων Ἑλλήνων ἀλλὰ καὶ κατὰ τὸ ἀρέσκον τοῖς θείοις μαθήμασι. καὶ δείξομεν ὅτι οὐχ οἷόν τε τούτους πολυθέους γενομένους ἐν χώρᾳ καὶ μερίδι κρείττονι γεγονέναι μετὰ τὴν ἐντεῦθεν ἀπαλλαγὴν, φέροντες τὰς περὶ αὐτῶν ἱστορίας, ἐν αἷς ἀναγέγραπται πολλὴ Ἡρακλέους ἀκολασία καὶ ἡ πρὸς τὴν Ὀμφάλην γυναικείως δουλεία, καὶ τὰ περὶ Ἀσκληπιοῦ ὡς κεραυνῷ βληθέντος ὑπὸ τοῦ Διὸς αὐτῶν. λελέξεται δὲ καὶ τὰ περὶ τῶν Διοσκούρων, ὡς ἄλλοτε μὲν ζώουσ᾿ ἑτερήμεροι, ἄλλοτε δ᾿ αὖτε τεθνᾶσιν· τιμὴν δὲ λελόγχασιν ἶσα θεοῖσιν οἱ πολλάκις ἀποθνῄσκοντες. πῶς οὖν οἴονται κατὰ τὸ εὔλογον τούτων νομισθῆναί τινα θεὸν ἢ ἥρωα;
pass_a_gloss: Leaving out (καταλιπών) no form (εἶδος) of disparagement (διασυρμός) and ridicule (καταγέλως) about us, the buffoon (βωμολόχος) Celsus in his discourse against us names the Dioscuri and Heracles and Asclepius and Dionysus, those believed (πεπιστευμένους) among Greeks to have become gods from men (ἐξ ἀνθρώπων). And he says that we do not endure (ἀνέχεσθαι) to consider (νομίζειν) these gods, because they were men, and first (καὶ πρῶτοι), although they displayed (ἐπιδειξαμένους) many and noble (γενναῖα) things on behalf of men; but we say that Jesus, having died, was seen (ὦφθαι) by his own fellow-revellers/devotees (θιασωτῶν); and he further accuses (προσκατηγορεῖ) us also as saying that he was seen, and that a shadow (σκιάν). And to these we shall say that Celsus cleverly/craftily (δεινῶς) neither clearly presented that he does not worship (σέβειν) these as gods (for he was cautious of (εὐλαβεῖτο) the opinion of those who would meet with (ἐντευξομένων) his writing, who would suppose him godless (ἄθεον) if he championed (ἐπρέσβευεν) something of the truth appearing to him), nor again did he pretend (προσεποιήσατο) himself to consider them gods; for to each of the two we would have answered. Come then, to those not considering them to be gods let us say these things: Do these not exist at all (οὐδὲ τὴν ἀρχήν), but, just as some think about the soul (ψυχή) of men as being destroyed (διαφθειρομένης) at once (παραχρῆμα), the soul of these also was destroyed? Or, according to the opinion of those saying it survives (ἐπιδιαμένειν) or is immortal (ἀθάνατον), do these survive or are they immortal, and they are not gods but heroes (ἥρωες)? Or not even heroes but simply (ἁπαξαπλῶς) souls? If then you suppose them not to exist, the account about the soul that is primary (προηγούμενον) for us must be established (κατασκευαστέον); but if they exist, so too the account about immortality (ἀθανασία) must be accepted (ἀποδεκτέον), not only from the Greeks who spoke well about it but also according to what is pleasing to (τὸ ἀρέσκον) the divine teachings (θεῖα μαθήματα). And we shall show that it is not possible that these, having been polytheists (πολυθέους), came to be in a better region and portion (χώρᾳ καὶ μερίδι κρείττονι) after the departure (ἀπαλλαγή) from here, bringing the histories (ἱστορίαι) about them, in which is recorded much licentiousness (ἀκολασία) of Heracles and the womanish (γυναικείως) slavery (δουλεία) to Omphale, and the things about Asclepius as struck by a thunderbolt (κεραυνῷ βληθέντος) by their Zeus. And there will be told also the things about the Dioscuri, that 'at one time they live on alternate days (ἑτερήμεροι), at another time again they are dead; and they have obtained (λελόγχασιν) honour equal to gods', those dying many times (πολλάκις ἀποθνῄσκοντες). How then do they think, according to reason (κατὰ τὸ εὔλογον), any of these to be considered a god or hero?
pass_b_english: Omitting no kind of disparagement and ridicule of us, the buffoon Celsus, in his discourse against us, names the Dioscuri, Heracles, Asclepius, and Dionysus, who are believed among the Greeks to have become gods after being men. And he says that we cannot bear to regard these as gods, because they were men to begin with, although they displayed many noble deeds on behalf of mankind; whereas we, he says, claim that Jesus, after he died, was seen by his own devotees. He further accuses us of saying that he was seen, and that, too, as a shadow.

To this too we will say that Celsus has craftily neither stated clearly that he does not worship these as gods (for he was wary of the opinion of those who would read his writing, who would take him for an atheist if he championed anything of the truth as it appeared to him), nor, on the other hand, pretended that he himself regards them as gods; for we would have replied to either position.

Come, then, let us say this to those who do not regard them as gods. Do these men not exist at all, their soul too having perished, as some think the human soul perishes at once? Or, according to the opinion of those who say that the soul survives or is immortal, do these survive or are they immortal, being not gods but heroes? Or are they not even heroes, but simply souls? If, then, you suppose that they do not exist, we must establish our primary doctrine about the soul; but if they do exist, then here too the doctrine of immortality must be accepted, not only from those Greeks who spoke well about it, but also in accordance with what the divine teachings hold.

And we will show that these men, who worshipped many gods, cannot have come to a better place and portion after their departure from this world. We will bring forward the stories about them, in which are recorded the great licentiousness of Heracles and his womanish slavery to Omphale, and how Asclepius was struck by a thunderbolt from their Zeus. The story of the Dioscuri will also be told, that “now they live on alternate days, and now again they are dead; and they have won honour equal to the gods” (Homer, Odyssey 11.303–304), they who die over and over. How then do they think it reasonable that any of these should be regarded as a god or a hero?

choices.choice: Celsus's statements are indirect speech in the Greek, so not in quotation marks; 'devotees' (θιασωταί, members of a cult band, originally of Dionysus) and 'shadow' are his terms, which Origen picks up in 3.23. Doubtful reading: ὅτι ἄνθρωποι ἦσαν καὶ πρῶτοι is odd Greek; rendered 'because they were men to begin with', taking it as stressing that they were first men and only later counted gods; a corruption (for example of πρῶτον) is possible. Several full stops printed mid-sentence in the staged text (after θεοὺς, πρῶτοι, σκιάν, γραφῇ, αὐτοὺς) are treated as commas. The switch to the second person plural (ὑπολαμβάνετε, 'you suppose') is kept. πολυθέους γενομένους rendered 'who worshipped many gods'. Homer, Odyssey 11.303-304: ἄλλοτε μὲν ζώουσ᾿ ἑτερήμεροι, ἄλλοτε δ᾿ αὖτε τεθνᾶσιν· τιμὴν δὲ λελόγχασιν ἶσα θεοῖσι, quoted verbatim (θεοῖσιν with nu). Heracles' service to Omphale, Asclepius struck by Zeus's thunderbolt, and the Dioscuri's alternate days of life are myths Origen names, not quotations; only the Homer lines are quoted. 'Zeus' and the pagan gods are lowercase 'gods'. No Scripture quoted or alluded to. τὸν δ᾿ Ἰησοῦν ... ὦφθαί φαμεν stays inside Celsus's report (φησιν governs it), so the English adds 'he says' to keep the speaker clear.
